p: [interposing] I've heard differently. That's what I'm asking. So go ahead. I've heard it takes about, you know, takes a while to get them hired, and therefore the season kind of moves along. But go ahead.

Thank you, Councilmember. No, we have no issues with— no constraints with hiring. We're very efficient at it. As the commissioner said, we have three tranches. We hire in mid-April for spring startup in ball field, May 1st for beaches, and June 1st for pools. So the last of those three tranches will be coming on within the next week, because again, we open pools in the end of June. So each of the tranches comes on about a month before their work is needed.
How about the— what I call horticulturalist or season people in the parks? Not—
That would be April 15th.
April— so they— and they start for the whole summer, and they're already on April 15th?
Yep, six-month lines that begin April 15th.
Alright, thank you.
Okay, great. So we've been joined by Council Member Won as well. So we have Council Member Narcisse followed by Council Member Won.

Thank you, Commissioner, and thank you for the leadership and everyone that's here. But it seemed like the question I was going to ask about the staffing again— do we have enough staff? I know you came with your dream, and so is the leadership here. So do we have enough staff, or do we need funding to make sure that all the things that we asking— because I'm going to ask too what we need in our district and New York City at large. Do we have enough funding to cover? You feel

like we're going to be— you're going to be able to run the parks safely with, you know, efficiency and everything?

Thank you for your question. I will again say that I'm extremely proud of the work that we're doing with the staff and resources that we've provided. I, of course, would always welcome more resources and more staffing. However, we also understand the mandate that we have and the responsibility that we have to deliver a safe, welcoming, open park system that is well cared for. And we'll continue to work on doing that with the resources that we have.

You know, we love parks, right? So, in 2024, in our adopted budget that we had, right, the plan was– we had $800,000 for a pilot program to provide menstrual products in the parks bathroom. Can you please give me an update on that?
Sure. I'll turn to our First Deputy Commissioner. Do you have any—

Yeah, my recollection is that I believe, in a series of PEGs, that might have

been— I can't remember the exact plan, but my recollection is that the funding for that pilot was withdrawn before the pilot started.
Oh, okay. So we're not going have menstrual products in our bathroom the way that we expected.
It is not a standard amenity.

Okay. Moving forward, we talk about pools in the city of New York. You know that a lot of areas we don't have any pools, including mine. One of the goal– because we talk about Shirley Chisholm a lot, and which I spoke to the commissioner. To me, rec center is just like a preventive approach when it comes to so many problems we're dealing with in New York City with our youth. So, in term of planning, like, for instance, right now, I push very hard to get a study done, and it's— in EDC right now. So I want to know how, Commissioner, I can push forward to make sure it happen. Not in 10 years ahead, but right now, what can we do to make sure it happen?

Thank you for your question, and let me just reiterate to you, I too believe very much so that our parks and our recreation centers are absolutely a part of— should be part of the public health discussion, should be part of the public safety discussions. So much of putting down places like Shirley, places like Mary Cali Dalton, the work that's happening at Walter Gladwin and other places, and in the Bronx and across the city, really does result in safer, more oper— safer neighborhoods, creating more opportunity, more upward mobility, and so many other things. And it's— it's a joy and a privilege to be able to do that. I'm grateful for your $500,000 that you've allocated to look through this, and I'm very happy to work with you on this. As you know, with something like Shirley Chisholm, we saw funding coming in from cities, from city and the state, I believe, in terms of making this a reality. I think that we should continue to have conversations, particularly now because we are able to show communities what can be possible when you have purpose-built spaces. When you have new spaces being built for modern-day recreation. And

when we say recreation, we know we mean so much more than just an athletic basketball court or a gym where— which is great, but we see so much more. We talk about arts, technology, and culture, and other pieces to this. So we're happy to continue to give— to work with you in terms of spreading that narrative of what recreation centers, what New York City parks and recreation centers actually mean. Which is way more than your gym space. It is— we're talking about economic development, we're talking about safer and healthier neighborhoods, and I'm happy to work on you— work with you and to champion that narrative.
Yeah, thank you, and I would like to be the catalyst to that process, because it takes so long.
Yes.

Everything that we have to do in parks is just forever, and that's the reason I'm with my colleagues, what can we do, because we feel like we are sitting, like, waiting and things not happening. It's just like– it's just frustrating to some level. Look at Shirley Chisholm. You have 11,000 new members already. I was there.

It's a beauty. So we can continue doing that. That's all I'm saying, because I'm here, right? I mean, ready to work with you. And even for the plants, like, we're talking about the trees, 2,900. If we can help, we have some kind of organization locally, maybe we can help speed up the process. That's all I'm saying. So thank you for your time and thank you, Chair.
Thank you. Okay, Council Member Won followed by Council Member Brooks-Powers on Zoom.

Thank you so much, Chair Lee. Good to see you, Commissioner. I want to— I have a few questions on some of my parks. So first and foremost, the capital tracker for parks is severely broken and is never updated. It's extremely frustrating for myself and all my constituents. So Murray Park was found to have severe remediation issues. It's the only dog park and playground in Court Square, and we're still waiting for that park to come online. Can you give us a clear update on when that park is going to come online and when it

will go into construction? Because it's been four years.

Yeah, thank you, Councilmember. I appreciate the comments on the capital tracker. I will have to get back to you specifically on the updates, which we will. We have a very good track record of following up with every request when it comes to these. So we'll happily give you that update. I'll happily look into this myself. But I wanted to tell you, with the capital tracker, I hear you. We want to make sure that the information is up to date, but also that is realistic on our timelines. Of course, sometimes we see those timelines slip back for whatever reason, but we'll look into this specifically and make sure that the information is as updated as possible.

Okay, because it's extremely important that that park comes back online and that all the soil is remediated. And next, as part of the One Long Island City rezoning project, the city committed to developing five acres of new public open space under the Queensborough Bridge by 2031, including $97.3 million in capital funding. The

capital plan states on page 113 that this commitment is funded through four different projects with planned commitment dates starting from June 31 to June 33. In correspondence with members of the parks planning team, we have received confirmation that this funding was supposed to begin in FY28 through FY31. So it is severely behind. So the project ID numbers are LIC, QNB, P2, SEED, S-E-E-D-QBAQ, SEED-OSQB, and then, SEED-QBBP. Can you clarify the start date for the capital funding for new open space under the Queensborough Bridge as promised? And will the funding timeline present any delays in the city's commitment timeline to the completed new open space by 2031, which is what we're assuming because of the dates that you've printed? And do you expect any additional funding to– will be needed to complete these projects given the timeline has been pushed back pointing to your latest print.

Sure, we'll, we'll have to again get— thank you for the specifics. We'll have to get back to you specifically on where those projects stand. However, I will tell you that I was just— and thank you. Frankly, let me just also

say thank you for your advocacy. I think that additional open space is always really exciting. I know that you fought very hard for this and specifically were really involved. I think that will– to my knowledge, and I was just briefed on this project recently, I have not heard of any delays. This year, so we'll have to get back to you to be sure of that. Sometimes we get that funding and it's allocated for funding in out-years, so that may be when funding is coming to us. But I have not heard to date any sort of delays with these projects. I know that they were very important. They were a big win for you, and we'll continue to give you updates on them.

Okay. And then the city also committed $30 million in renovations to renew Queensbridge Park as part of One LIC rezoning, with design beginning in FY28. And the capital plan dates on page 113 that this project is funded with planned commitment dates of June 32. So again, another delay, far beyond what was promised to us and committed to when we– in writing. In correspondence with members of the parks planning team, we have

received confirmation that this funding was supposed to begin in FY28 through to FY32, project ID SEED-QBRG. Can you clarify the start date for the capital funding to renew Queensbridge Park? And will funding timeline present any delays to the city's commitment timeline to begin design FY28? And do you expect any additional funding to complete this project? Because the Speaker, Adrienne Adams, the former Speaker, has also committed $12 million to this project, and this is extremely vital for the largest public housing community members to have access to this park on time.

I'll interject here, just for a moment to clarify. With every financial plan, the agency worked closely with OMB to go through what we call a rationalization exercise, which is when the capital fundings are actually placed in the fiscal year in which they are expected to be registered. So the vast majority of a capital project's budget gets spent down during construction. So therefore, when a project begins, that means it starts design. But then there is the expected design time, the expected procurement time,

you know, other additional time. So it is, very common, and in fact necessary, that the relevant funds, the bulk of the relevant funds, will be placed in an out-year. So it's, you know, as the Commissioner I think noted that, but just to provide additional clarity, that sort of spreading out of capital funds is extremely common, not specific to those projects whatsoever, happens throughout our capital portfolio.

Okay, great. I just want to make sure that it's on record that the Queensbridge, under the Queensbridge Park, it will be completed by June 2031, and also the Queensbridge Park itself will be completed by– will begin design in FY28 and be completed by '32. So I just want to have that on record, and I will follow up with you via email to make sure that we are continuing to keep this project accounted for. Thank you so much.
Okay, great. Okay, unfortunately we lost quorum, so we're going have to skip ahead to Council Member Wong followed by Council Member Nurse.
Thank you, Chairs. Thank you, Commissioner, for coming. We'll be chatting later on the phone.
Yes, we will.

Yes. My first round of question is regarding the biggest park in my part of Queens, in my district, Juniper Valley Park, particularly the bathrooms and capital project that's involved. Right now, Juniper Valley Park currently has zero functioning bathrooms. One building is out of service due to an active capital project, and the other closed recently due to unforeseen circumstances, something to do with the sewer line. This park is heavily used by seniors, families, and children, especially during the summer, and we have an upcoming concert in a couple days, this Thursday, and then we need the bathrooms. Can your agency give this Council today a firm completion date for the station house bathroom near the tennis court? Because we need it.
Sure.
Yes.

Thank you for your question, and I will just say that I'm in— we are incredibly proud to be the largest agen— the agency that provides the vast majority of public restroom buildings throughout the entire city, over 700. That's more than there are Starbucks in the city. It's a tremendous responsibility that we take very seriously. So we'll get back to you specifically on the updated date of the restroom project that's going on in your district. But I want to also flag that we can also— I would love to work with you, Council Member, offline to see about– I'm of course concerned about big gatherings happening in the parks when there's no public restroom building available. We can look at whether like some sort of porta-sand [sic] situation or something else that can– could be– happen there. Oh, there are already. Great. So I know that we're– we– it sounds like we have some porta-sands or some other temporary toilets there. It's not ideal and it's certainly not the long-term strategy, but we want to make sure that we are also working closely with you to accommodate these big events when they're happening.

That's what— that's my next question, because it took— it took me several phone calls to finally get temporary sanitation facilities, and the answer I was told was the cost of these temporary porta-potties are not baked into any capital projects, and how would park attendees go to the bathroom if if there's no budget for these porta-potties. And in this case, this is serious because we have this huge park and both bathrooms are closed. And first we asked and asked, only two porta-potties were provided, and only recently another two. And this— we're still asking for more because in an average concert we have 400 or 500 people going, and four porta-potties is clearly inadequate. And that's my question. Why— why are porta-potties not budgeted into capital projects? Because it makes no sense.

You know, it really— and I appreciate the question, and I'm glad to hear that we're working with your office, and we work with others. I was just talking to another council member, I think Aviles, about porta-sans in her District 2. While we have– while we have a

capital project going on. It's difficult to bake something like that into our contracts, one, because I don't actually know if that's a capital eligible piece to it, but two– it's not. And then two, every park project is different. We may have a park where we have one capital project going on where it doesn't require it because there's another porta— there's another public restroom building in that park, so they would be able to find the bathroom elsewhere, while as some we think are going be– are going to be handled in the wintertime where we think it can handle it, versus others where unfortunately at Juniper Park you have kind of, unfortunately all the bathrooms are down at one time. So it's difficult for us to predict and it's also not capitally eligible. So it's unfortunately not something that we're able to do. But I will say that I'm– you know, we are very sensitive towards wanting to make sure that even when these capital projects are happening, that communities are still able to use their parks. So in the cases like this, I'm very happy to hear that we're providing those public— those temporary public

bathrooms is not the ideal situation, but at least there's something there.
So we'll talk later about this, and there's some other issues that we need to resolve with you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Great. Thank you. And next we have Council Member Nurse, and then the Chair will be asking Council Member Brooks-Powers' questions.

Thank you. I'm going to talk about my district parks because that's what we do at parks hearings. But, I want to say Highland Park, amazing. Thank you. I always love the maintenance and attention given there. Tiger Playground, great. I have no issues. My issues are at Irving Playground and Irving Square Park and Bushwick Playground behind Bushwick Campus. And that is where I need, at least for Bushwick Campus, extraordinary attention this summer for enforcement. I've done years of walkthroughs. There's 1,000 emails to you all. You all know about this area. Last summer, we had a couple stabbings. It was really bad. All the

time, it was a source of nonstop complaints, and Bushwick Campus, that park, we really need attention this year. So, I don't know how many PEP officers you have in Brooklyn. Every time I call and ask, there's like only 12 in the whole borough or whatever. I don't know where we're at now, but we do need extraordinary attention this summer. I'm only asking for one park to have attention, and it is that park. The 83rd does what they can for it, but we really, we really need attention there. With Irving, it's less about enforcement, but I do often see a lot of our volunteers pushing non-electric mowers to mow the grass. I mean, it would be great if we could get the grass cut on time. I don't know if there's a schedule, but I hate to see that. I mean, I love people doing their part, but I don't want these folks having to mow the grass in our little park. And then we have a bathroom there now. So I'd love to talk with you all about a Playground Associate there, and also making sure that that bathroom is stocked on a regular basis, because we've gotten a lot of complaints about that.

Yeah, thank you so much, Council Member. Let me just thank you so much for your comments. I really appreciate it. We can certainly look at Bushwick and Irving. I wrote those down. I just want to clarify that for our PEP staffing, we have 53 staff members that are baselined for Brooklyn, 53 in the Bronx, 53 in Manhattan, 53 in Queens, 32 in Staten Island. Again, that's for the entire borough. So do you—
[interposing] How many are assigned to North Brooklyn?
I would have to get back to you.

Yeah, I would love to know. Every time I call, it's like we only have five people on. I just can never get anybody there. Yeah, I'm always call the precinct, call the precinct, and the precinct's busy, you know.

Absolutely. And I will say also that I know that that doesn't feel– it has a very different feeling as well when it comes to also we see our, our PEP officers who are, that are then at our pools and at our beaches. And so they do

cover a lot of ground and we're very proud of every single one of them.
I understand.
You had mentioned in terms of bathrooms and mowing, so I wanted to just mention the grass.
Yeah, just getting the grass cut.

Yeah. So, certainly while we're have— we do have a regular schedule. I'll look to our First Deputy Commissioner to share a little bit more about that regular schedule of grass cutting. If there's anything in particular that we're not seeing, we appreciate your feedback on that.
Well, I always let— I always let the Brooklyn Commissioner know when it's time, but it would be nice to not have to do that.
Yep.
Thank you.

And then for the bathrooms, our— I'll ask our First Deputy Commissioner also to speak on this, but we do monitor

everything from soap to toilet paper to working fixtures in our public restroom buildings. So we will certainly look at this because it would be coming up. We monitor this on a regular basis, and we're happy to have the First Deputy Commissioner speak more to this.

Council Member, the site should be mown on a two-week cycle. Okay, so we'll look into it. We track the data. I can look at a dashboard. As the Commissioner said, our public restrooms— we have three touch points a day at every one of our public restrooms because we unlock them in the morning, check to make sure they're stocked, they're cleaned at least once a day if not more times, and then obviously at the end of the day we close them. So there's a minimum of three touch points. So there shouldn't— there may be any moment in time when we may have gone in, stocked, and it, you know, it happens regularly.

I understand. I understand sometimes you go in there and clean it, an hour later it doesn't look like that. I get it. I just— I'm advocating for attention there. There have

been many nights we've had events there. We've let parks know, hey, we're going to have an event there, can you make sure the bathroom's open, make sure it's stocked? It's not open, it's not stocked, we got to chase people for an hour. It's just like some– it's just some like baseline of maintenance I think would be– especially when we proactively let you know about certain things going on in the park. We'd really love just some attention this summer because I don't really ask much for Parks, just those two. Thank you.
Thanks.

Okay. Alright. I'm just going– you can put the timer on. I'm going to ask questions on behalf of Council Member Brooks-Powers who's online. The Executive Plan includes a baselined increase of about $121,000 of city funding beginning in FY26 for lifeguards covered by the additional compensation fund, CBA. How many vacant lifeguarding positions remain across New York City? And if you can just answer, you know, very quickly.

Yeah, very quickly. Okay, so we– so we are funded for 1,400

lifeguards. We— that's our— we have said that that was pre-pandemic our height. We last year were at 1,100, a little less than 1,100. We won't have our final numbers until later on this July. Things are looking very good. We're very optimistic about hitting a higher number than we were at last year. At this point in time last year compared to now, we are at higher numbers. So we'll be able to fully answer that and give kind of our full numbers by the 4th of July.
Thank you. With this baseline increase, does Parks intend to increase the number of staff lifeguards?
I'm sorry, can you repeat that question?
With this baseline increase, does Parks intend to increase the number of staff lifeguards?
Yeah, sorry, I believe it's a— so it was a collective bargaining. So it's sort of essentially a pay increase, so not a headcount change.
Given the recent drowning deaths on Rockaway Beach, how does the Parks Department intend to prioritize lifeguard staffing for the Rockaway Peninsula this summer?

Sure, let me just say before I pass it over to our First Deputy Commissioner who oversees the lifeguard division, that we are incredibly sad to see this– the drowning that happened at Rockaways. I want to thank the NYPD and FDNY and Emergency Management, of course our lifeguards who are all there and looking into this further. I just want to use this as an opportunity because I have yet to say it, but I want to just ask all of our elected officials' help in reminding everyone that it is only safe to swim in our water when there's a lifeguard sitting in a chair, when they're saying that it is okay to swim. Otherwise, you should not be in the water. It is incredibly important to remember this as kind of a simple rule of thumb. When it comes to our overall water safety plan, this is something that is— has been truly kind of honed in over years of experience, over years of working with colleagues and looking at other

operations across the country. Truly, we believe in our water safety plans. We believe in our water safety protocol. We are looking to fully— to again, follow through on our lifeguard plan that we had last year, and it was tremendously successful. But I'll look to our First Deputy Commissioner to give more details.

Council Member, as I mentioned earlier, as of today we have 153 lifeguards at Rockaways, which is more than twice the next closest beach, which is 70 at Coney Island. We traditionally staff— of all of our beach lifeguards, which is about 600 when we're at our peak, over 55 percent of them go to the Rockaways, 45 percent cover our other seven beaches. So the majority of our lifeguards always go to the Rockaways.

Thank you. How much funding does Parks Department have allocated for the Trees and Sidewalks program to repair severe sidewalk damage caused by root growth? We have heard from constituents that the wait time for this program

takes years. What is the agency doing to expedite this service?

Yes, thank you so much. We have– we do have a program that is– it deals with trees and sidewalks concerns for qualifying qualifying applicants. The funding is $13 million, which allows us to repair approximately 1,300 sites per year.
Are you planning to explore the implementation of an emergency system along Rockaway Beach?

You know, we have had a lot of conversations about this. We are always interested in looking at additional ways to get emergency alerts out there to increase water safety. Rockaway Beach is particularly difficult because there's not, to our knowledge, a system that can allow for the five-plus miles of boardwalk to receive that notification system through the PA system. That has been discussed. We're happy to continue to look at this. We do have an audio system at Orchard Beach, which is much smaller. So if there is a system out there that can, like, provide this, we're happy to

continue to look into it. Rockaway Beach is a very large beach in order to cover all of that. So always interested in additional notification systems. It's just the size of it is really difficult to find a system that can work. I'll let our First Deputy Commissioner add more to that.

I would just note that we're always pushing notification communications out through NYC Notify for folks that subscribe to that. We really emphasize that frequent beachgoers, particularly folks in the Rockaways, should subscribe to NYC Notify. And also, as you're aware, we're purchasing new emergency response vehicles specifically for our lifeguards to use on the sand to respond to emergencies.

Thank you. Final question. This is from Council Member Shanel Thomas-Henry. The Executive Plan includes an additional $1.7 million for 200 additional seasonal positions due to the World Cup. The Queen's Fan Fest is in her district in Flushing Meadows, Corona Park. How many of those positions are for this event in

particular, and is any effort being made to hire locally for those positions?

So our— so we're very excited about and grateful for the 200 positions that will be able to bring on onboard as of the start of the fiscal year. I think that they are truly— we always use, when it comes to deploying staff, a data-driven approach towards looking out for our sites that are most in need and we know are going to be hotspots. So we'll continue to be in communication around where those staff go to. But I want to just say a huge thank you to the administration and OMB for understanding that our parks are where everybody is going to be this summer. It is going to be an incredibly busy summer in our parks. It always is, but with— but a lot of the best viewing locations are going to be in our park system, and we'll be continuing to have— being in close communication with NYCEM and others about where we expect to see the largest crowds.

Thank you, Commissioner. I'm sorry, there was one more question, final question from Council Member Brooks Powers, and

I'm going to turn it over. On May 12th, the council member sent a letter to the Parks Department regarding compliance with Local Law 132 of 2023. The law requires the city to survey city-owned property that may be suitable for the construction of new public swimming pools and release survey results by October 1st, 2025. Despite repeated outreach by the council's compliance division to DPR, DOE, and City Hall, Council still has not received any report, nor has the administration told the Council which agency will be responsible for the implementation of Council Member Brooks-Powers’ sponsored Local Law. Can the agency please provide an update on the compliance with this law?

Yes, thank you for the question. My recollection is that the bill as dra— as passed required the mayor's office to designate a, you know, an entity to lead the effort. We're going to have to circle back to mayor's office and get an update. My understanding is an entity to this point in time had not been identified.
Okay, great. And next we have Council Member Krishnan before we go to round two.

Thank you, Chairs, and good to see you, Commissioner and team, as always, and all the parks advocates here. I just had a couple of questions to follow up on some points that were already discussed. But my first one is, it is concerning to see the underfunding of PEP officers in the budget so far. And I just want to get an understanding. So normally we have 300 PEP officers, which we know not enough for the whole city, 60 per borough. As of right now with the Executive Budget, only 200 have been funded. OMB and the Council are pushing for another 100 on top of that. Is that— is that right?

Your numbers are almost— are almost there. So, 354 officers total. That's including 100 of our one-shot officers. So, in the case where— which we hope would not happen, but we— in the case where we would not get that one-shot funding either baselined or in one-shot, then we would lose those 100 lines. But currently, I think

the, like, discussion has been whether or not those 354— those 100 officers could be baselined into, like, into fully into our ranks. And then of course, we would of course always welcome additional PEP officers through new one-shot.
Right, right. Okay. And so right now, those 100— so those are, you know, obviously officers right now who are funded— their positions are funded only through June 30th of this year, correct?
Yes.

And then without a one-shot or without them being baselined, their positions would not exist after July 1st, right? I mean, I know that Parks will make every other effort to find other places for them, but I just want to get an understanding of what that would mean for PEP starting July 1st.
Sure. I mean, that's with every single one-shot position. We are only funded through the fiscal year, and after that, that's— there's no more funding.

Yeah, yeah. I mean, obviously, the first and foremost, and I've always said this too, the Parks budget is such fundamentally a workers' budget. I know they're— they are all, as workers, very concerned about their positions. What have the conversations been like, to the best that you can share, with City Hall and OMB? Because there— with all that's going on in our parks this summer, and you're hearing it from, you know, everyone too, whether it's the World Cup, whether, you know, it's NBA Finals and other park celebrations and things like that, it is concerning that we haven't been able to get the PEP officer count much higher. And so what have the conversations been with City Hall and the OMB so far? And how does Parks plan to adequately staff the parks across the borough when there's basically, at best, 60 officers per borough?

Yeah, thank you for your question. Our conversations have been pretty robust and ongoing and overwhelmingly positive, I'd say. I believe that this administration understands the impact that our PEP officers bring. I'm very grateful for the advocacy of the Council, yourself of

course included, and many parkies know how much you fought for us, and so we are grateful to you. I think that we also understand that it is our— it is our absolute goal to serve our city regardless of the actual number of resources. So whether it be with our– with our current ranks now, or, you know, unfortunately in a situation where we would have fewer staff, we will continue to— we will continue to meet the mission that we have. I would say overwhelmingly this administration understands the absolute incredible impact that parks have and the role, the vital role that we play in creating an affordable city, an affordable future for our city, and I'm very proud to continue to uphold that. Thank you, and look forward. Thank you for your kind words. Also looking forward to working with you all and City Hall to make sure we get that number to where it needs to be. And then just the hiring freeze– in the Preliminary Budget time, we talked about the hiring freeze. What is the status of lifting that hiring freeze at this point? How is that looking so far? And what more can you comment on?

Yeah, very good. I mean, honestly, we are— we're very— we were, as many other agencies I'm sure will say, we're very excited about having the two-for-one kind freeze lifted and having the ability to actually fill the vacancy spots that we have when they become available. I'm very grateful to OMB. We've worked— we had a lot of conversations about the 40 positions that were kind of vacancies in our ranks and are very much looking forward to being able to— right now we're pretty much full, but as– what we also see on any given month, just through nature of attrition and retirements and things like that, we see empty spaces, empty seats come up across the agency, and it is very exciting to think about a world in which we get to hire for those seats.

Great, glad to hear it. And then just concluding by just saying I'm glad to hear the progress on the lifeguard issue. There's a big crisis. A lot more to do on that. You know, any ways that we can work together to keep increasing lifeguard count. One of the things that I've been focused on, and we can talk more about it,

you know, later too, is, you know, not only sta— fully staffing our pools and beaches, but I also feel like our pool and beach season is too short given how warm it's getting earlier in the year, how warm it stays later in the year. And, you know, it would really help a lot if we can extend pool and beach season.
